title: Classification system for cervical spine deformity morphology: a validation study
condition_or_topic: Morphological classification of cervical spine deformity
clinical_background: As cervical deformity progresses, patients may have difficulty keeping the head aligned over the pelvis and maintaining a horizontal gaze; spinal cord compression may also impair balance and coordination. Maintaining gaze can require substantial effort and adversely affect quality of life. The clinical significance of sagittal alignment in cervical deformity remains under investigation. Because cervical deformities vary considerably, a consistent classification could support systematic study and treatment planning. No universally accepted classification exists. An earlier system by Ames et al. was established by surgeon consensus, whereas Kim et al. identified flat neck, focal deformity, and cervicothoracic patterns from static and dynamic plain radiographs. The latter system had not yet been validated.
objectives: Provide an initial validation of the cervical spine deformity morphological classification developed by Kim et al., adding a group whose predominant deformity is coronal.
Assess the classification’s reliability and accuracy across physician training levels.
interpretation: The morphological classification of cervical deformity showed moderate to substantial reliability. Its accuracy did not vary significantly with reviewer experience, which the authors interpret as evidence of its simplicity. Accuracy was 73.5% when reviewers selected one category and rose to 86% when either of two principal deformity drivers counted as correct. The authors interpret this increase as reflecting the complexity of deformities with more than one important component.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Ames et al. reported moderate interobserver and intraobserver reliability for their cervical deformity classification, with Fleiss kappa coefficients of 0.489 and 0.584, respectively. In the present study, interrater Fleiss kappa was 0.563 in round 1 and 0.612 in round 2, and the intrarater score was 0.686. The authors suggest that the higher interrater reliability may reflect differences in what the two systems classify; they consider the similar intrarater findings evidence that reviewers classified cases consistently. Unlike the consensus-derived categories of Ames et al., the earlier Kim et al. system was developed from patterns identified in radiographic data. Prior studies cited by the authors also linked changes in CL to outcomes in thoracolumbar scoliosis and surgery for cervical myelopathy; those outcomes were not assessed here.
clinical_implications: The findings support further development of a shared morphological framework for organizing cervical deformity patterns and, potentially, planning treatment.
Dynamic plain radiographs are important when evaluating cervical deformity because the classification draws on how cervical alignment changes with movement.
A deformity may have more than one principal driver, so a single category may not capture its full presentation.
practice_implications: Consider dynamic plain radiographs when evaluating patients with cervical deformity.
Consider multiple contributing deformity patterns rather than assuming that every case has only one driver.
limitations: All reviewers came from one tertiary spine center, limiting the immediate generalizability of the validation findings.

Reviewers had to select one deformity pattern even when a patient had secondary drivers; allowing multiple selections might have increased accuracy but would not have tested identification of the primary driver in the same way.
Cases were retrospectively reviewed from a database whose patients had been preselected for study enrollment by clinicians or researchers.
The validation sample comprised 38 patients. The authors considered a larger set potentially fatiguing for reviewers.
Radiographs came from multiple centers, so flexion-extension imaging protocols could not be standardized.
Supine plain radiographs were not obtained, although they might have provided further information about deformity flexibility.
strengths: The reviewer panel included physicians at different training levels.
Reviewers had not participated in the original classification-development study.
The authors consider the cohort representative of the range of cervical deformity and the reviewer panel sufficiently large for this initial validation.
open_questions: How best can the morphological classification guide surgical treatment?
Whether the radiographically defined subgroups respond differently to nonsurgical or surgical treatment remains to be established.
future_directions: Investigate how the classification can inform surgical strategies for different deformity patterns.
Develop a morphology-based approach to surgical intervention, potentially for use when conservative measures fail.
study_design: Initial validation of a cervical deformity morphological classification using a retrospective selection of preoperative radiographs from a prospective multicenter database. The database comprised patients operated on between 2013 and 2015 at 13 participating centers. A panel of 15 physicians classified randomized cases as flat neck, focal deformity, cervicothoracic, or coronal deformity. The cases were re-randomized for a second classification round 7 days later. Reviewers received the publication describing the classification groups.

population.description: The sample comprised 38 adults with cervical deformity: 10 consecutive patients in each of the flat neck, focal deformity, and cervicothoracic groups, and 8 with coronal deformity only. Reviewers were 5 orthopedic surgery residents, 3 spine surgery fellows, and 7 spine fellowship–trained attending surgeons. Each case was assessed using preoperative standing full-length anteroposterior and lateral spine radiographs and cervical plain radiographs in anteroposterior, neutral lateral, flexion, and extension views.
inclusion_criteria: Cervical deformity defined by at least one of the following: cervical kyphosis with C2–7 sagittal Cobb angle > 10°, cervical scoliosis with C2–7 coronal Cobb angle > 10°, C2–7 sagittal vertical axis (SVA) > 4 cm, or CBVA > 25°.
population.care_setting: Patients were drawn from 13 participating surgical centers; physician reviewers came from a single tertiary spine center.

comparators: Flat neck, focal deformity, cervicothoracic deformity, and coronal deformity morphotypes.
Reviewer training levels: residents, spine fellows, and attending surgeons.

primary: Interrater and intrarater reliability of the morphological classification, assessed with Fleiss kappa.
Classification accuracy, defined as correct identification of the principal driver of deformity.
secondary: Reliability and accuracy by reviewer training level.
Accuracy when identification of either of two principal deformity drivers counted as correct.

statistical_methods: Demographic characteristics and sagittal alignment in neutral, flexion, and extension were summarized using means and standard deviations (SDs), medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), or rates for categorical variables. Sagittal alignment was compared across deformity types with ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests. Fleiss kappa quantified interrater reliability for all reviewers and by training level, and intrarater reliability for individual reviewers, summarized by mean values overall and by training level. Kappa interpretation used 0.00–0.20 for slight, 0.21–0.40 for fair, 0.41–0.60 for moderate, 0.61–0.80 for substantial, and 0.81–1.00 for almost perfect agreement. Accuracy was assessed overall, by morphotype, and by reviewer experience, with an additional analysis of cases with combined deformity drivers.

subgroup_analyses: For round 1 interrater agreement, residents had Fleiss kappa 0.547 (95% CI 0.527–0.567), spine fellows 0.600 (95% CI 0.572–0.628), and surgeons 0.524 (95% CI 0.515–0.533); the authors described agreement as similar across training levels.
Mean intrarater kappa by training level was 0.715 for residents, 0.640 for fellows, and 0.682 for surgeons.

With one category counted as correct, accuracy differed by deformity type: flat neck 67.3%, focal 84.7%, cervicothoracic 68.7%, and coronal 73.3% (p = 0.002). Accuracy was lower for flat neck and cervicothoracic deformities than for focal deformity.
With one category counted as correct, accuracy by training level was 75.0% for residents, 78.1% for spine fellows, and 71.1% for attending surgeons.

When either main deformity driver counted as correct, accuracy by type was flat neck 90%, focal 86.7%, cervicothoracic 91.7%, and coronal 82.5%; accuracy exceeded 80% for every type, and the between-type difference was no longer significant (p = 0.078).
When either main deformity driver counted as correct, individual reviewers' accuracy ranged from 68.4% to 100%, and 12 raters had accuracy > 80%.

Accuracy was lower in patients with a secondary deformity driver: 50% of raters selected the first driver and 50% selected the secondary driver. Cases with accuracy below 75% generally drew responses into two main classification categories.

main_conclusion: The authors found that the cervical deformity morphology classification had overall reliability and that reviewer experience did not affect its overall accuracy. They emphasize dynamic plain radiographs in evaluating cervical deformity and state that further study of surgical strategies for the different patterns is needed.
narrative_summary: This study initially validated a morphological classification of cervical deformity comprising flat neck, focal deformity, cervicothoracic deformity and a coronal group. Investigators selected preoperative radiographs from 38 patients in a prospective multicenter database. A panel of 15 physicians—residents, spine fellows and attending surgeons—classified every case twice, with the cases re-randomized after seven days. Interrater agreement was moderate to substantial: Fleiss kappa was 0.563 (95% CI 0.559–0.568) in round 1 and 0.612 (95% CI 0.606–0.619) in round 2. Mean intrarater agreement was 0.686. Reviewers answered 419 of 570 classification questions correctly (73.5%) when a single primary category was required. Accuracy rose to 86.0% when selection of either of two main deformity drivers counted as correct. Under that approach, accuracy exceeded 80% for every morphotype, and differences by reviewer training level were not significant (p = 0.432). The authors interpret the findings as support for the classification’s reliability and simplicity, while stressing the value of dynamic plain radiographs. They note that all reviewers came from one tertiary spine center, the validation sample was small, and flexion-extension imaging protocols could not be standardized across centers. Further research is needed to establish how the morphological groups should guide surgical treatment.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVE
document_sections.content: The study sought an initial validation of a recently developed morphological classification for cervical deformity (CD).

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: Investigators selected records from a prospective multicenter CD database: 10 patients in each of the flat neck, focal deformity, and cervicothoracic subgroups, plus 8 patients with coronal deformity only. A panel of 15 physicians, comprising residents, fellows, and surgeons, assigned each case to one of the 4 groups. Fleiss kappa was used to assess agreement between and within raters. Accuracy meant identifying the principal driver of deformity and was examined overall, by morphotype, and by reviewer experience.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Agreement between raters was moderate to substantial: round 1 interrater Fleiss kappa = 0.563, 95% CI 0.559–0.568; round 2 interrater Fleiss kappa = 0.612, 95% CI 0.606–0.619. Mean interrater coefficients by training were residents 0.547, fellows 0.600, and surgeons 0.524. Mean intrarater agreement was 0.686 (range 0.531–0.823); 81.8% of raters had substantial agreement across rounds 1 and 2, with kappa > 0.61. Mean intrarater coefficients were residents 0.715, fellows 0.640, and surgeons 0.682. Reviewers answered 419 of 570 possible questions correctly (73.5%). Counting identification of at least one of two principal deformity drivers raised overall accuracy to 86.0%.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: This initial validation supports the overall reliability of the CD morphological classification and emphasizes dynamic plain radiographs in CD evaluation. Reviewer experience did not affect overall accuracy, which the authors interpret as evidence of the system’s simplicity.

document_sections.heading: Classification system for cervical spine deformity morphology: a validation study
document_sections.content: As CD advances, patients can lose head-over-pelvis alignment and struggle to sustain a horizontal gaze. Spinal cord compression can also impair balance and coordination. The effort required to preserve horizontal gaze adversely affects quality of life. Smith et al. found, using the EQ-5D index, a substantial health impact across age groups compared with an age-matched normative US population; patients’ mean index was below the bottom 25th percentile reported for other chronic conditions, including malignant breast cancer, malignant prostate cancer, and chronic ischemic heart disease. Although global sagittal alignment has received attention in thoracolumbar deformity, its role in CD remains under investigation. Recent studies associate changes in cervical lordosis (CL) with outcomes in thoracolumbar scoliosis and surgery for cervical myelopathy. The chin-brow vertical angle (CBVA), a measure of horizontal gaze, has been correlated with overall disability. Understanding of sagittal alignment and outcomes after CD surgery is still developing. Pathological heterogeneity may undermine CD research without an organized approach. Other spinal classifications supply shared terminology, support treatment decisions, and provide a foundation for evidence-based care, but CD has no universally accepted classification. Ames et al. introduced a common CD framework incorporating global spinopelvic malalignment and clinically relevant measures; its categories, however, were set a priori by surgeon consensus and were not linked to health-related quality-of-life (HRQOL) measures. Kim et al. hypothesized that severe CD subgroups differ according to sagittal alignment and used static and dynamic cervical radiographs to define clinical groups. Their two-step cluster analysis identified 3 sagittal patterns: flat neck, focal deformity, and cervicothoracic deformity. Because this classification uses plain radiographs without requiring advanced imaging, it may be applicable across care settings. Better recognition of principal deformity drivers may assist preoperative assessment and initial treatment planning, but the system had not undergone validation needed for its use in evaluation, diagnosis, and surgical treatment. This study therefore aimed to validate the classification initially, adding a fourth group for predominantly coronal deformity. The authors hypothesized that reliability and accuracy would hold across training levels.

document_sections.heading: Study Sample
document_sections.content: The sample came from a prospective multicenter database of patients who underwent CD surgery between 2013 and 2015 at one of 13 participating centers. Database eligibility required age of at least 18 years and at least one defining feature: cervical kyphosis with C2–7 sagittal Cobb angle > 10°, cervical scoliosis with C2–7 coronal Cobb angle > 10°, C2–7 sagittal vertical axis (SVA) > 4 cm, or CBVA > 25°. A multi-institutional expert panel determined and confirmed broad CD classification for database entry. Active tumor or infection excluded patients. This investigation used preoperative images only. Each patient had full-length standing anteroposterior (AP) and lateral spine radiographs, plus AP and neutral lateral cervical radiographs with flexion and extension views. Measurements from 36-inch long-cassette spine radiographs included pelvic incidence (PI), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, pelvic tilt (PT), C7-SVA, and T1 pelvic angle (T1-PA). Cervical images provided C2–7 Cobb angle/CL, cervical SVA (cSVA), C2 slope (C2S), T1 slope (T1S), and T1S-CL. Investigators also measured maximum focal kyphosis between adjacent segments and counted kyphotic levels with an angle > 5°. Flexibility was the absolute difference between a lateral-view measurement and its extension-view counterpart. Measurements for all patients were made at a single center using validated spinal-alignment software. Following the original classification publication, the team selected 10 consecutive cases per sagittal subgroup and 8 cases with coronal deformity only. Patients treated surgically at the authors’ institutions were excluded, and no author had cared for the presented cases.

document_sections.heading: Panel Review for Classification Validation
document_sections.content: For every case, reviewers received full-length AP and lateral spine radiographs and AP, lateral, flexion, and extension cervical radiographs, together with global, cervical, and focal sagittal measurements. Case order was randomized rather than grouped by morphology. The 15 physicians classified each case as flat neck, focal deformity, cervicothoracic, or coronal. Residents were randomly chosen; all spine fellows and surgeons at the senior author’s institution were included. Reviewers received the Kim et al. publication describing the groups. After 7 days, cases were randomized again and the panel repeated classification by the same approach. Every panel member classified every case in both rounds.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Demographic and neutral, flexion, and extension alignment data were summarized with means and standard deviations (SDs), medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), or rates for categorical variables. Sagittal alignment comparisons across morphotypes used ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests. Fleiss kappa assessed agreement within and between raters. The stated agreement bands were 0.00–0.20 for slight, 0.21–0.40 for fair, 0.41–0.60 for moderate, 0.61–0.80 for substantial, and 0.81–1.00 for almost perfect agreement. Interrater results were reported for the full panel and by training level; intrarater results were calculated per reviewer and summarized as means overall and by training level. Accuracy was correct identification of the principal deformity driver and was evaluated overall, by morphotype, and by reviewer experience. For cases with combined drivers, a further analysis counted selection of at least one principal driver as correct.

document_sections.heading: Cases
document_sections.content: Among 38 patients with CD, mean age (± SD) was 63.8 ± 11.0 years (range 40.0–83.7 years), and mean BMI was 28.8 ± 7.7 (range 18.5–5.0, as reported). TABLE 1 presents cohort demographics by group, and TABLE 2 compares cervical sagittal-plane radiographic measurements across morphotypes. Imaging was assessed by 15 reviewers: 5 orthopedic surgery residents, 3 spine surgery fellows, and 7 attending surgeons trained in spine fellowships.

document_sections.heading: Reliability Testing
document_sections.content: Overall classification yielded moderate to substantial interrater agreement: round 1 Fleiss kappa = 0.563, 95% CI 0.559–0.568; round 2 Fleiss kappa = 0.612, 95% CI 0.606–0.619. In round 1, reliability was similar across training groups: residents 0.547, 95% CI 0.527–0.567; spine fellows 0.600, 95% CI 0.572–0.628; and spine surgeons 0.524, 95% CI 0.515–0.533. Of 15 raters, 11 reclassified every case for the intrarater assessment. Mean intrarater kappa was 0.686, ranging from 0.531 to 0.823. Substantial agreement between rounds 1 and 2, defined here as kappa > 0.61, was seen in 81.8% of raters. Mean intrarater coefficients by training were residents 0.715, fellows 0.640, and surgeons 0.682.

document_sections.heading: Accuracy
document_sections.content: Reviewers made 419 correct selections among 570 possible questions (73.5%); TABLE 3 summarizes classification accuracy. Single-category accuracy differed by morphotype, with lower performance for flat neck and cervicothoracic than for focal deformity: flat neck 67.3%, focal 84.7%, cervicothoracic 68.7%, and coronal 73.3%; p = 0.002. Accuracy was lower when a secondary deformity driver was present: 50% of raters chose the first driver and 50% chose the secondary driver. Most cases with accuracy below 75% attracted two dominant groups of answers, such as focal deformity with a coronal component. Accepting either of two principal drivers increased overall accuracy from 73.5% to 86.0%. Under that approach, accuracy exceeded 80% for every morphotype and no longer differed significantly among types: flat neck 90%, focal 86.7%, cervicothoracic 91.7%, and coronal 82.5%; p = 0.078. Individual-rater accuracy for identifying at least one main driver ranged from 68.4% to 100%, with 12 raters exceeding 80%. Training-level differences were not significant: residents 86.2%, fellows 89.5%, and surgeons 84.5%; p = 0.432. An illustrated focal-deformity case had 100% reviewer accuracy. Another illustrated case had 60.7% accuracy: it was classified as flat neck because of its large T1S-CL (TS-CL) and some compensation on extension, while focal kyphosis between laminoplasty levels was a secondary driver. Cases of this kind often split reviewers between two principal classifications.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors intended to validate terminology for organizing CD patterns systematically and potentially aiding future treatment planning. They interpret the observed reliability as moderate to substantial and the lack of an accuracy difference by reviewer experience as supporting the classification’s simplicity and broad applicability. Because CD causes substantial disability, they regard improved understanding of sagittal and coronal alignment in diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment as important. Previous studies reported that changes in CL affect outcomes in thoracolumbar scoliosis and in patients undergoing surgery for cervical myelopathy. Classification systems may support treatment decisions and evidence-based care; this study assessed a system grounded mainly in clinical patterns and static and dynamic cervical radiographic findings. The authors describe the Ames et al. system as the other comprehensive CD classification. Adapted from the Scoliosis Research Society–Schwab adult thoracolumbar classification, it requires full-length standing AP and lateral spine images including the cervical spine and femoral heads, standing posteroanterior and lateral cervical images, a clinical photograph or skull-inclusive radiograph for CBVA measurement, and modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association scale scores. The authors credit that system with establishing common CD terminology but note that its groups were defined a priori by surgeon consensus. They cite evidence that its CBVA and T1SCL modifiers are not specific to CD and may appear in asymptomatic people without altered HRQOL. By contrast, Kim et al. developed a data-driven, predominantly sagittal-alignment classification through two-step clustering combining hierarchical and k-means methods. That numerical method identifies naturally occurring dataset groups. Dynamic radiographs largely defined the resulting subgroups by showing whether patients can correct cervical sagittal alignment; those groups might respond differently to nonsurgical and surgical treatment. The Ames et al. classification reported moderate interobserver and intraobserver reliability, with Fleiss kappa coefficients of 0.489 and 0.584, respectively. With a similar analysis, the present study found interrater kappas of 0.563 in round 1 and 0.612 in round 2, and intrarater agreement of 0.686. Both studies supplied angular measurements to reviewers, which aided reliability, although neither classification requires specific radiographic measurements or thresholds for assigning a group. This study also assessed aspects not reported for the Ames et al. classification. The authors suggest that their higher interrater agreement may reflect the emphasis on an overall morphological pattern: an Ames et al. subgroup represents only one component of that system and can fall within different groups of the Kim et al. system. Similar intrarater findings in the two studies suggest consistency in reviewers’ own CD groupings. Requiring one category produced overall accuracy of 73.5%. Because CD can involve more than two deformity types, cases below 75% accuracy often produced two leading answer categories. Allowing either of two principal drivers increased overall accuracy to 86%, underscoring the complexity of CD and the need to consider multiple features. Similar accuracy among orthopedic residents, spine fellows, and fellowship-trained attending surgeons was interpreted as further evidence of simplicity; the authors identify simplicity and cross-training-level accuracy as important features of clinically useful spinal classifications. They view initial validation as a step toward evidence-based CD care and suggest that morphological groups could inform development of surgical interventions after conservative measures fail. Limitations include recruiting all reviewers from one tertiary spine center, which restricts immediate generalizability, although they did not participate in the original classification-development study. Reviewers had to choose one pattern despite secondary drivers in some cases; permitting multiple answers might have improved accuracy but obscured findings about the primary driver. Some trainee reviewers had not belonged to that center when the classification was created. Cases came from retrospective review of a database containing patients preselected for study enrollment by clinicians and/or researchers. The 38-case validation sample was small, although the authors judged that adding cases could fatigue reviewers. Because patient radiographs came from different centers, flexion-extension imaging protocols could not be standardized. No supine plain radiographs were obtained, although these might have captured further CD flexibility. The authors nevertheless consider the cohort representative of the CD range and the reviewer panel large enough for validation. They see the results as another step toward a morphology-based surgical algorithm. Future research is needed to establish how the classification should guide surgical treatment.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The initial validation reinforces the value of dynamic plain radiographs when evaluating CD and supports the morphological classification’s overall reliability. Reviewer experience did not affect overall classification accuracy, which the authors take as evidence of simplicity. Further examination of surgical strategies across the different patterns is needed to guide the most effective treatment.
